title: Privacy policy
description: How Yuppers.app collects, uses, shares and keeps information about the people who use Yuppers.
note: This policy describes how Yuppers.app works today.

links.smsOptIn: how people opt in to texts from Yuppers.app

blocks.p: This policy explains how Yuppers.app (https://yuppers.app) collects and uses your information. Yuppers.app (“we”, “us”) runs Yuppers, a service for writing, signing and keeping track of two-person agreements, called yups, on the website yuppers.app and in the Yuppers app. Below we explain what information we collect, how we use it, who sees it, how long we keep it, and the choices you have.
Yuppers is offered in the United States, to adults 18 and over, in English and Spanish. Our servers and our database are in the United States.
Using Yuppers is also governed by our {terms}.
For any question or request about your privacy, write to {privacyEmail}.

what-we-collect.title: What we collect and how we use it

blocks.p: We collect what Yuppers needs to work, and use it only to run Yuppers. For each kind of information below, we say what it is and how we use it. We don’t use analytics, advertising or tracking tools, and we don’t build profiles of you. We do not sell your personal information. We do not share your personal information or your SMS opt-in data and consent with third parties or affiliates for marketing or promotional purposes.

ul: Your email address, your phone number, or both. We send one-time sign-in codes to them (by text when available, through our provider Twilio’s verification service, Twilio Verify), we email you when something happens in one of your yups, and, if you turn on text updates for an agreement, we text your phone number when its status changes.
Your name, as you want the people you make yups with to see it.
Your language (English or Spanish), so that the product, our emails and our codes reach you in it.
That you confirmed you are 18 or over, and when. We don’t ask for your date of birth.

When your account was created, and your sign-ins: how you proved it was you (a code by email or by text message), when, and until when each one lasts. We use these to keep you signed in, and to end your sign-ins when you sign out or delete your account.

What you and the other person write and do in each yup: its terms; each item, with what is given, how much, by when, and how you’ll both know it’s done, including any amounts of money you name; the names of both people as the proposal gives them; every version sent; messages, notes and statements; each signature; and what each of you records about delivery. Keeping this is the point of Yuppers: it is the shared record of what you agreed and what happened.
Drafts you are still writing. We save them as you go so that you don’t lose them.

What you tell us about the other person. Whoever writes a proposal gives both people’s names, and may give the email address or phone number the invitation is for. We use that address to check that the person who opens the invitation is the one it was meant for. If someone signed in with another address opens it, we tell them only whether it was sent to an email address or a phone number, never the address itself. If they type it and it matches, and only then, we send a one-time code there, so that they can add it to their account and open the invitation; we never send anything else to it. We keep it only as a keyed hash.

blocks.p: When you sign, we record your account, how you proved it was you (a one-time code by email or text message) and when, the time you signed, a fingerprint (hash) of the exact terms you signed, and which version of the consent wording you were shown, in which language. We also record the IP address your request came from and the description your browser or app gives of itself (its user agent). These are evidence of the signature. The IP address and the user agent are deleted after {networkDays} days, and the app never shows them to anyone; the rest of the signature stays with the agreement.

If you report a yup or a proposal, we keep your report: the reason you chose, what you wrote, who sent it, and which yup and person it is about. We use it to review the report and act on it. If you block someone, we keep who you blocked and when, and use it to keep that person out of yups with you. When a report is reviewed, we keep a history of what the reviewers looked at and decided, to keep review accountable.

blocks.h: Text updates for an agreement, if you turn them on

blocks.p: If you turn on text updates for an agreement, we keep a record of it: which agreement, the phone number, when you turned them on, and the consent wording you were shown. We use it only to send you those updates and to show that you agreed to receive them. With it we keep the language the wording was in and whether you used the website or the app, and, for {networkDays} days, the IP address and user agent of your request, as we do for a signature. We also record when updates are turned off, whether by you, by a STOP reply, by a change of your phone number or by deleting your account, and every STOP and START we receive from a phone number.

blocks.h: Codes by text, when available, if you ask for one

blocks.p: When you ask for a one-time code by text, to sign in, to confirm deleting your account or to add a number to your account, we keep a record that you ticked the box beside your number (the code itself is made and checked by Twilio Verify): what the code was for, the version of the wording beside the box and its language, whether you used the website or the app, and when. If the number is already your account’s, we keep it and your account with the record. If it isn’t yet, the record keeps only a keyed hash of it: a fingerprint, made with a secret key, that lets us find the record from the number if we are asked about a text, but that can’t be turned back into the number. (The record of the code itself keeps the number only as a keyed hash too, for about a day, as “One-time codes” below says.) For {networkDays} days we also keep the IP address and user agent of your request, as we do for a signature. We use the record only to show that you asked for the text we sent.

blocks.h: Notifications in the app, when available, if you turn them on

blocks.p: If you turn on notifications in the Yuppers app, we keep your device’s push token, its platform (iOS or Android), the app’s version and your language, so that we can send notifications to that device.

blocks.h: Wallet passes, when available, if you add one

blocks.p: If you add a yup to Apple Wallet or Google Wallet, we keep a record of the pass: which yup and account it belongs to, and how it was last updated. For Apple Wallet we also keep the identifiers and push tokens that Apple gives us for the devices that hold the pass, so that we can keep it up to date. A pass shows the yup’s reference code, its status, how many items are still to do, and a link back to the yup. It never shows the terms, names or amounts.

blocks.h: Payment options, if you add them

blocks.p: If you choose to save payment options on your account (a Venmo username, a Cash App $Cashtag, a PayPal.Me name, or the email address or US phone number you use for Zelle), we keep them encrypted, as we do email addresses and phone numbers. Saving them shows them to nobody. If you turn them on for a yup, the other person in it sees them while they owe you money there, as buttons that open those apps. We don’t send your payment options to those apps or to anyone else: when the other person taps a button, their own device opens the app with your username, the amount and a short note (the item’s title and the yup’s reference) filled in where the app allows. A Zelle option has no button; it is shown as it is, for them to copy, and it is often your own email address or phone number. We don’t put payment options in emails, texts, notifications or Wallet passes, and we don’t move or receive money. We also keep when each payment option last changed: if one changed after the yup came into force, the other person sees a warning beside it. We never keep the earlier value. Any payment happens in the app, between the two of you, under that app’s own terms; we only record what each of you says about it.

ul: Request logs. For each request our service answers, we log the method and the path (never the query string), the status, how long it took, and a request ID. We use them to run the service and to find and fix problems. Our logs never contain what was sent or answered, codes, tokens, email addresses, phone numbers or IP addresses.

Sign-in limits. To stop anyone from guessing codes or asking for too many, we count the codes asked for from each IP address and the wrong codes entered for each email address or phone number; the codes to confirm deleting an account asked for, and the wrong ones entered, for each account; the tries at the address an invitation was sent to, for each account and for each invitation; and the texts we send, and the codes by text we don’t send (because a limit was reached, the number’s country isn’t served, or our provider refused it), for the whole service and for each group of numbers that begin alike (by area code). These counts are stored under a keyed hash, never the IP address, the email address, the number or the account itself. With your saved payment options we also count how many times your account changed them in the last hour, to limit how often that can happen.

One-time codes. For a code by email, we store a keyed hash of the code, never the code itself, with a keyed hash of the email address it went to and when. For a code by text, Twilio Verify makes and checks the code, and we store a record that one was asked for: a keyed hash of the phone number, what the code was for, when it was asked for, until when it works, and how many wrong codes were entered for it. Once Twilio Verify accepts a code you enter, we add a keyed hash of that code to the record, never the code itself, so that the same code still works if you have to try again before it expires. We use these records to check the code you enter, and to limit how many codes are sent and guessed. Each record, with the keyed hash of the email address or phone number in it, is deleted about a day after the code was asked for, once the code has expired or been used.

cookies-and-storage.title: Cookies and storage on your device

blocks.p: The website uses one cookie and three pieces of browser storage, all to make the product work. There are no analytics, advertising or tracking cookies, and no scripts from anyone else.

ul: yuppers_session (a cookie): keeps you signed in. It holds a random token, lasts until about {sessionIdleDays} days after you last use the site, up to {sessionMaxDays} days, or until you sign out, and the page’s scripts can’t read it.
yuppers.language (local storage): the language you picked, so that the website opens in it next time.
yuppers.theme (local storage): your appearance choice (System, Light or Dark), if you picked one, so that the website opens in it next time.

yuppers.invitation (session storage): the code from an invitation link while you sign in to read it, so that reloading the page doesn’t lose it. It is removed once the invitation is opened or turns out to be no longer valid, and when you close the tab.

blocks.p: In the Yuppers app, your sign-in is kept in your device’s secure storage (the iOS Keychain or the Android Keystore), with your notification setting for that device. Your appearance choice (System, Light or Dark) is kept in the app’s own storage on the device. A copy of a record that you choose to share is kept in the app’s cache only until you make the next copy or sign out.

Besides you, your information is seen by the other person in each yup, as far as the yup shows it; by the people who review reports, while a report is open; and by the companies that help us run the service.

blocks.h: The other person in a yup

blocks.p: The other person sees what the yup shows: its terms, every version, the messages and notes, its history, the signatures and when they were made, and your name as the agreement gives it. They don’t see your email address, phone number, IP address or device, except an email address or phone number you save as your Zelle payment option, which they see as that option where you turn your payment options on. Each of you can download or print the yup’s record, and what each of you does with that copy is up to you. If you turn on your payment options for a yup, they also see those, while they owe you money in it, until you turn them off.

Reviewers we name can see a report, the names and account status of the people it involves, and the whole record of the yup it is about, but only while the report is open. Every report a reviewer opens, and every decision, is written to a history that can’t be changed. Nobody reviews a report they are part of.
The people who run Yuppers can also reach the database directly, to operate and back up the service and to answer requests like yours.
We use these companies to run Yuppers. Each receives the information needed for the job described:

ul: Render hosts our service, our database, our server logs and the database’s backups, in the United States.

Cloudflare runs our domain’s DNS and carries every request to yuppers.app over its network before it reaches Render, so it handles your IP address and the request. It may ask your browser to report connection errors to it. It also forwards email sent to our addresses, such as {privacyEmail}.

Resend sends our emails, from the United States, so it receives your email address and the email: a one-time code, or a notice that something happened in one of your yups (which never includes the terms). Resend sends them through its own infrastructure provider, Amazon Web Services (Amazon SES), and keeps its own copies of the emails and of their delivery records for 30 days.

Twilio, when we send text messages, receives your phone number and the message: an agreement update, if you turned them on; and, through its verification service, Twilio Verify, for each one-time code by text, your number, the code it makes and sends you, the code you enter, and the language to write it in.

Expo, Apple and Google, if you turn on notifications in the app: Expo receives your device’s push token and the notification and passes them to Apple’s or Google’s push service, which delivers it. A notification only says “Your yup has an update.”, with the yup’s internal ID so that the app can open it.
Apple and Google, if you add a Wallet pass: Apple delivers the pass’s updates to your devices, and Google keeps the pass (its status, reference code and number of items) to show it in Google Wallet.

blocks.p: We don’t share your information with anyone else, except where the law requires us to. We don’t sell it, share it for advertising, or let anyone use it for their own marketing.

When we offer them, Yuppers.app sends text messages in one program, Yuppers.app agreement updates, and for nothing else: no marketing. One-time codes by text are not part of that program: our provider Twilio sends and checks them with its verification service, Twilio Verify.

ul: Yuppers.app agreement updates: if you turn on text updates for an agreement, by ticking a box on that agreement, we text you when its status changes, for example when the other person signs, marks something delivered, confirms it, disputes it, or asks to close it, and once when you turn them on, to confirm. Message frequency varies; there is no fixed maximum: one text per status change of an agreement you turned updates on for. An update says only that something changed, with a link to sign in and see it. It never includes the terms, amounts or names of goods, just as our emails and app notifications don’t. If you turn on detail on your account page, a text or phone notification also says who the yup is with and which step happened; it never carries the terms.

One-time codes by text: a code to sign in (which also creates your account the first time), to add a number to your account, or to confirm that you want to delete your account. We ask Twilio Verify for one only when you ask for a code, and only for the number you entered or, to confirm a deletion, the number on your account. Entering your number, ticking the box beside it that says what will be sent, and asking for a code is your request for that text; until the box is ticked, nothing is sent. Twilio Verify makes the code, texts it to you and checks the code you enter. Message frequency: one message for each code you ask for.
Message and data rates may apply.

**Reply HELP for help.** **Reply STOP to stop receiving texts from us.** A STOP sent in reply to an agreement update stops all texts from Yuppers.app to your number, agreement updates and one-time codes alike, so you’ll need to sign in with an email address instead. A code comes from one of Twilio’s numbers, so a STOP in reply to a code goes to Twilio, not to us. Turning off text updates for one agreement stops the updates for that agreement only.

Phone numbers outside the United States are not texted: we send texts only to US numbers, which start with the country code +1 and the area code of one of the 50 states or Washington, D.C. Numbers in Canada, in the Caribbean and Pacific countries and the US territories that share +1, and toll-free numbers, are not texted.
We do not sell your personal information. We do not share your personal information or your SMS opt-in data and consent with third parties or affiliates for marketing or promotional purposes.
Mobile information will not be shared with third parties or affiliates for marketing or promotional purposes.
Mobile information and opt-in consent are not shared with third parties or affiliates for marketing or promotional purposes.

To deliver the texts, we give your phone number to our SMS provider, Twilio, and to no one else: with each agreement update, its text; and for each one-time code, to Twilio Verify, the language to write it in. Twilio Verify makes the code it sends, and receives the code you enter so that it can check it.
Carriers are not liable for delayed or undelivered messages.

blocks.p: For help with text messages, write to {supportEmail} or reply HELP to any agreement update. For privacy questions, write to {privacyEmail}. The terms of the program, and of one-time codes by text, are in our {terms}.
Every step of opting in, with the exact wording of each screen and each message, is shown on the page on {smsOptIn}.

ul: Your email address, phone number, name and language: while you have an account. Deleting your account removes them from it at once. Your phone number then stays only where “What stays, and why” below says: in the record of text updates you turned on and of codes you asked for by text, as proof of what you agreed to, and, if it replied STOP, on our list of numbers we must not text.

Yups that were sent, with everything in them and their history: we keep them as the shared record of what was proposed and agreed. We don’t delete them when one or both people delete their accounts, and we have not set a time after which they are deleted.
Drafts you haven’t sent: until you send them, discard them or delete your account.
Payment options you save: until you remove them or delete your account. Turning them off for a yup stops showing them there at once.
The email address or phone number an invitation is for: only a keyed hash, for as long as the yup is kept.

An account combined into another: its ID, with no email address, phone number or name, for as long as the yups and reports that refer to it are kept. An email about your account (that two accounts were combined, or that an email address was changed or removed), with the address it went to: {combineNoticeDays} days. A proof, from a one-time code, that you control one of your account’s email address or phone number, which adding or changing one needs: usable once, for 10 minutes, and deleted a day after that.
The IP address and user agent recorded with a signature: {networkDays} days.

The record of text updates you turned on for an agreement, and of their ending: for as long as the updates are on, and then for {smsConsentYears} years after they end, as proof that you asked for the texts we sent. The IP address and user agent recorded with it: {networkDays} days. A phone number that replied STOP: for as long as it stays unsubscribed, so that we don’t text it again.
The record of each code you asked for by text: {smsConsentYears} years, as proof that you asked for it. The IP address and user agent recorded with it: {networkDays} days.

One-time codes: each code works for {codeMinutes} minutes, and only once. A code by text works for {codeMinutes} minutes from when it was first sent, and asking again within that time resends the same code. The record of a code (a keyed hash of where it went, when, and the code’s hash where we keep one) is deleted about a day after the code was asked for, once it has expired or been used; deleting your account deletes the ones for your email address and phone number at once.

Sign-ins: each lasts until about {sessionIdleDays} days after you last used Yuppers, and no more than {sessionMaxDays} days after you entered the code, unless you sign out first. Then you need a new code. The record of a sign-in is deleted {endedSessionDays} days after it ends.
Sign-in limit counts: two days.
Request keys: the random key the website or the app sends with each change, so that a change sent twice is made only once, is deleted {idempotencyKeyDays} days after the request.

Notifications: the record of each email, app notification or text we queue for you (which notice, about which yup, and how sending it went; never its text, your email address or your phone number) is deleted {notificationDays} days after it was queued, once it was sent or we gave up sending it.

Push tokens: until you turn notifications off, your sign-in on that device ends (when you sign out, when it expires, or when you delete your account), or the push service tells us the token no longer works.

Wallet passes: the record of a pass stays with its yup; when you delete your account, your passes are voided. The device identifiers Apple gives us are removed when a device removes the pass, and no later than 30 days after a pass is voided.

Reports, and the history of how they were reviewed: kept, including after an account is deleted, so that leaving doesn’t erase a complaint. Blocks you make: until you unblock the person or delete your account.
Server logs: kept by our hosting provider, Render, for up to 30 days.

Backups: our hosting provider, Render, keeps copies of the database for recovery, in the United States, for up to 7 days. We keep no other backup copies; if that changes, this policy will say where and for how long. If we ever restore a backup, we first delete again every account that our deletion log shows was deleted, taken from the live database or, if it is lost, from the newest copy of the log we have, so a deleted account stays deleted. If the database itself were lost, a deletion made after the newest copy we have could be lost with it; if your deleted account ever comes back, write to {privacyEmail} and we will delete it again. A copy made before we started encrypting email addresses and phone numbers holds them unencrypted until it expires.
The deletion log: when an account is deleted, we keep its account ID and the time, and nothing else, so that a restored backup can’t bring it back.

blocks.p: You can delete your account yourself, at any time, from your account page on the website or in the app. To confirm it’s you, we send a one-time code to your email address or phone number that only works for deleting your account. A number that replied STOP gets no texts from us, codes included, so if your account’s only way in is such a number, reply START to one of our texts first, or write to {privacyEmail}. A suspended account can’t be deleted from the account page, since it can’t sign in; to delete one, write to {privacyEmail}. Deleting can’t be undone.

ul: You’re signed out on every device.
Your email address, phone number, name and language are removed from the account.
Your one-time codes, the devices registered for your notifications, drafts you haven’t sent, notifications waiting to be sent to you, and your list of people you’ve blocked.
Text updates you turned on for your agreements stop.
Invitation links you made that nobody used stop working, and forget the address they were for.
Your Wallet passes are voided.
Your payment options, and their being shown on any yup.
Accounts you combined into yours: what is left of them, their sessions, goes too.

blocks.h: What happens to yups that are still open

ul: A draft you haven’t sent is discarded.

A proposal waiting to be signed ends with nothing agreed. The one exception is a proposal whose invitation you had opened and whose sender hadn’t yet confirmed you: you leave it instead, anything you signed in it no longer counts, and it stays open for its sender, who is told and can invite someone else.
An agreement in progress gets a request to close, made in your name. The other person is told and has time to respond, and then it closes as unresolved.

Yups that were sent stay with the other person, as the record of what was proposed and agreed: the terms, the history, your signature, and your name exactly as the agreement gives it. Your name in those records is not removed or replaced.
The IP address and user agent recorded with your signatures, until {networkDays} days after each signature.

The record of text updates you turned on, and that they ended when you deleted your account, with the phone number they went to, for {smsConsentYears} years, as proof of what you agreed to; and, if your number replied STOP, that it did, for as long as it stays unsubscribed. Every STOP and START we receive from your number is also kept, with the number encrypted, for {smsConsentYears} years (a STOP longer, while the number stays unsubscribed).
The record of each code you asked for by text, with your account and, where the number was on your account, the number, for {smsConsentYears} years, as proof that you asked for it.
Reports you made, or that were made about you, and the history of their review.

An account record with no contact details and no name: its ID, when it was created and when its holder confirmed being 18 or over, which the signatures it gave rely on; and its line in the deletion log.
Backup copies, until they expire as described above.

blocks.p: You can sign up again later with the same email address or phone number. That is a new account, with none of your old yups.

ul: See your information: your account page shows your email address, phone number, name and language, and each yup shows everything in it, with its whole history.

Combine two of your accounts: if you add an email address or phone number that is already on another of your Yuppers accounts, the code we send to it shows that both are yours, and we offer to combine that account into the one you are signed in to. What happens is described below.

Correct it: you can change your name and language on your account page, and add, change or remove your email address or phone number there, each with a one-time code. Adding or changing one, or combining another account into yours, also takes a code sent to one already on your account, so that being signed in is not enough to add a way in or take one away; and for 24 hours after one is added, a code to it can’t remove or replace one your account had before it. When an email address is changed or removed, we email it to say so; we don’t text a phone number about it, and your account shows the notice the next time you open Yuppers instead. Your account always keeps one of the two, since it is how you sign in; removing your phone number stops your text updates. A name changed there is used from then on; agreements already sent keep the names they were written with.
Take a copy: you can download each yup’s record as a file, or print it or save it as a PDF.
Delete your account: from your account page, as described above.

Notifications in the app: turn them on or off on the app’s account screen, or in your phone’s settings. Emails about your yups are how we tell you that something needs you, so there is no setting to turn them off; we never send marketing emails.
Text updates for an agreement: turn them on or off on that agreement’s page, or reply STOP to any of our texts to stop them all, and START to allow texts again.
Add a phone number: if your account has none, add a US mobile number from “Text updates” on a yup’s page, with a code we text to it.
Payment options: save, change or remove them on your account page, and turn them on or off for each yup on its page.

blocks.p: For anything you can’t do yourself, such as getting a copy of your information or asking a question about this policy, write to {privacyEmail}. We may need to confirm that a request comes from you before we act on it.

When you combine accounts, it can’t be undone. The other account’s yups move to yours, with everything signed in them kept exactly as it was signed and as signed by that account. The email address or phone number you added moves to your account, and so does the other account’s other one if yours has none of that kind; otherwise yours stays and the other account’s is removed. Its text updates continue if its phone number moves, and stop otherwise. Its payment options move only if your account has none, and are then shown as just changed to anyone who owes you money. Its Wallet passes, the people it blocked and the blocks against it move too; a block between the two accounts is dropped. It is signed out on every device. Afterwards the other account has no email address, phone number or name, and nobody can sign in to it. We keep its ID, linked to your account, because the history of its yups, and any reports by or about it, refer to it. We email every email address either account had to say the accounts were combined; that email says nothing about your yups, and we keep the address it goes to for {combineNoticeDays} days. We don’t text phone numbers about it: if neither account had an email address, your account shows the notice the next time you open Yuppers instead. If you later delete your account, what was the other account goes with it.
Residents of some states may have additional rights under their state’s laws. You can make any privacy request at {privacyEmail}, and we will respond.

Yuppers is only for adults 18 and over. Everyone confirms that they are 18 or over when they set up their account, and nobody can sign a yup without that confirmation. We don’t knowingly collect information about anyone under 18. If you think someone under 18 is using Yuppers, report it from the yup (“Someone under 18 is involved”) or write to {privacyEmail}.

ul: Connections to Yuppers are encrypted (HTTPS), and browsers are told to use nothing else.

We store one-time codes, sign-in tokens, the codes in invitation links and Wallet authentication tokens only as hashes, never as they are. Codes by text are made and checked by Twilio Verify, and we keep at most a hash of one, once Twilio Verify has accepted it.

We store email addresses and phone numbers encrypted, under a key we keep apart from the database, so the database or a copy of it doesn’t show them. Where we only need to find or compare one (to sign you in, to check who an invitation is for, or to keep to a STOP), we use a keyed hash of it instead. We decrypt them to send you an email, a code or a text, to show you your own, to encrypt them again under a new key when we replace ours, and to show them partly hidden where someone must tell who an account is: to the person who sent an invitation, who sees who opened it; to someone combining two of their accounts, who sees the other account’s; and to us, in our list of who reviews reports.

We store payment options you choose to save encrypted in the same way, and decrypt them only to show them to you and to the other person in a yup where you turn them on, and to encrypt them again under a new key when we replace ours.
The service uses a restricted database account that can add to an agreement’s history but can’t change or delete it, and the database itself refuses changes to that history.
Only reviewers we name can see reported yups, only while the report is open and after signing in within the last 12 hours, and every report they open is recorded.
Our logs leave out personal information such as email addresses, phone numbers, codes and tokens.

blocks.p: No system is perfectly secure, and we can’t promise that information will never be reached by someone who shouldn’t have it. If you think your account has been misused, write to {privacyEmail}.
When the way Yuppers handles information changes, we update this policy and post the new version on this page, with a new effective date at the top.
